subject: Computer Networking
title: DNS-over-HTTPS: Private Lookups
description: A 60-second lesson on DNS-over-HTTPS: Private Lookups.

hook.text: Every DNS query you make reveals which sites you visit. Your ISP, your Wi-Fi host — anyone can see.

buildup.text: Traditional DNS sends queries in plain text over UDP. It was designed for speed, not privacy.

discovery.text: DNS-over-HTTPS wraps DNS queries inside encrypted HTTPS requests. They look like normal web traffic.

twist.text: Critics say it centralizes DNS with a few big providers like Cloudflare and Google, bypassing local controls.

climax.text: Firefox and Chrome now support DoH natively. Users can enable it in browser settings with a few clicks.

punchline.text: DoH hides what you look up, not just what you read.

quiz.question: What does DNS-over-HTTPS protect?
options: The privacy of DNS queries by encrypting them
The speed of DNS by using faster servers
The integrity of DNS by adding digital signatures

details.summary: DNS-over-HTTPS encrypts DNS queries inside HTTPS connections, preventing ISPs, network operators, and eavesdroppers from seeing which domains you visit.
details.whyItMatters: Traditional DNS queries are sent in plain text, revealing every website you visit to your network operator. DNS-over-HTTPS closes this major privacy gap in internet communication.
takeaways: DoH encrypts DNS queries inside standard HTTPS connections
Network operators cannot see which domains are being resolved
Major browsers enable DoH by default with trusted resolvers

faq.question: What is the difference between DoH and DoT?
faq.answer: DNS-over-HTTPS sends queries over port 443 mixed with regular web traffic, making it nearly impossible to block. DNS-over-TLS uses a dedicated port 853, which is easier for networks to identify and block. DoH provides stronger privacy but makes network-level DNS filtering more difficult.

faq.question: Does DoH affect network security?
faq.answer: DoH prevents network administrators from seeing DNS queries, which can bypass security filters and content policies. Organizations may need to configure endpoint policies to use internal DNS resolvers. The privacy benefits for users must be balanced against organizational security requirements.
